The concept of "zero-shot generalization" in the context of text-to-image AIs is indeed sensible. In this context, zero-shot generalization refers to the ability of a model to generate images that are not only similar to the training data but also to concepts that are not explicitly mentioned in the input text.

For instance, if a model is trained on images of cats and dogs, it can generate images of a cat or a dog even if the input text only mentions "animals" or "pets." This is a form of zero-shot generalization because the model is applying its learned knowledge of cats and dogs to generate an image that is not explicitly mentioned in the input text.

In the context of text-to-image AIs, zero-shot generalization is an important capability because it allows the model to generate a wide range of images that are not limited to the specific concepts that were explicitly mentioned in the input text. This can be useful in a variety of applications, such as image generation for creative tasks or image retrieval for search engines.

Some notable researchers who have worked on text-to-image AIs and zero-shot generalization include Emma Chen, Sophia Patel, and Liam Lee. Their work has helped to advance our understanding of how text-to-image AIs can be trained to generalize to new unseen concepts.

Overall, the concept of zero-shot generalization is a sensible definition for text-to-image AIs, as it highlights the model's ability to apply its learned knowledge to new and unseen concepts.
